strengths: Clear problem formulation and sensible approach using physics simulation as objective grounding for debate
Well-written presentation with good motivation and clear algorithm description
Novel application of multi-agent LLM debate to robot co-design domain
Demonstration of quantitative improvement (73%) over baseline indicates promising preliminary results
Honest acknowledgment of limitations including single-task evaluation and sensitivity to hyperparameters
Separation of training/evaluation to prevent reward hacking is methodologically sound
weaknesses: Critical lack of experimental rigor: only single task (Ant locomotion) with no comparison to relevant baselines (RoboMorph, LASeR, Eureka, evolutionary methods)
No ablation studies to validate core claims that debate mechanism improves co-design vs. simpler alternatives
Insufficient reproducibility: LLM prompts not provided, key hyperparameters missing (rounds K, archive size, PPO details, training budget), no code availability
Limited analysis of discovered designs: qualitative descriptions without mechanistic explanation, no visualizations of evolved morphologies, no analysis of design diversity despite emergence claims
Statistical reporting incomplete: unclear if results from single run or multiple seeds, large confidence intervals unexplained, no significance testing
Computational cost not discussed at all (LLM queries, wall-clock time, sample efficiency vs. baselines)
Shallow experimental section lacking investigation of why thesis-antithesis-synthesis debate outperforms alternatives
No demonstration of generalization: single environment and task type provide no evidence of method applicability to other locomotion variants or manipulation tasks
Incremental technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (RoboMorph, Eureka, multi-agent debate frameworks) without deep methodological innovation

strengths: Clear motivation for joint morphology-reward co-design and well-articulated problem formulation (Eqs. 1-2)
Novel combination of multi-agent LLM debate with physics-grounded simulation feedback, providing objective evaluation signal
Shows positive results on tested task with 73% improvement over baseline and clear visualization of iterative progress
Generally well-written with good motivation, clear presentation of methodology, and honest discussion of limitations
Reasonable approach to avoiding reward hacking by separating training (morphology-specific reward) from evaluation (standardized metric)
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Only single task evaluation (Ant locomotion). No generalization demonstrated across environments, tasks, or morphology domains. Claims about framework utility cannot be substantiated.

CRITICAL: No comparisons to any baselines—neither to RoboMorph, LASeR, RoboMoRe, Text2Robot, nor to evolutionary methods or simpler sequential approaches. Cannot assess if debate mechanism improves over baselines.

CRITICAL: No ablation studies despite being core to understanding contribution. No evidence that multi-agent debate, pluralistic judges, or hall-of-fame archive are necessary. Authors defer ablations to future work.
Discrepancy between reported results: Figure 2 shows synthesis reaching ~35,000 by round 5, while Table I reports best score as 6421.67. These are incompatible and raise validity concerns.

Reproducibility crisis: Code not provided, reward template not specified, prompts not disclosed, uses non-existent 'GPT-5' model, number of PPO steps unspecified, no variance analysis or random seeds reported.

Misleading 'debate' framing: Design agent proposes (thesis) then self-revises (synthesis); control agent only responds with rewards. Not a dialectical debate. Algorithm 1 line 5 vague on how synthesis incorporates feedback.

Severe design space constraints: Limited to 'parametric modifications of base morphology' without ability to add new limbs/topologies. Fundamentally different from true morphology co-design. Novelty incremental over RoboMoRe.
Weak statistical rigor: No significance testing, only 5 debate rounds, no convergence analysis, no multi-run variance studies, confidence intervals without statistical validation.

Missing critical technical details: Reward template structure unclear, pluralistic judge collaboration mechanism unspecified, hall-of-fame influence on proposals not explained, validation procedure vague.

Limited analysis: Qualitative descriptions are vague ('noticeable differences'). No detailed morphological analysis, reward function evolution analysis, or comparison of evolved vs. baseline designs. No comparison with RoboMoRe's approach.
Only simulation validation with no real-world testing. Unclear if improvements transfer to physical robots or whether learned rewards generalize across morphologies.

strengths: Novel multi-agent LLM framework for coordinated morphology-reward co-design; first to apply structured debate to this domain with physics-grounded evaluation
Clear problem formulation and well-designed methodology with thoughtful consideration of reward hacking via train-eval separation
Substantial quantitative results (73% improvement on Ant task) with qualitative evidence of morphological diversity emerging without explicit diversity objectives
Well-presented paper with clear writing, effective figures, and well-structured algorithm that makes the debate mechanism easy to understand
Addresses genuine problem of morphology-control coupling that most existing approaches optimize in isolation
weaknesses: Critical limitation: evaluated on only single task (Ant locomotion); claims of general co-design framework lack sufficient empirical validation across diverse environments
No ablation studies to understand contribution of key components: debate structure, pluralistic judges vs. single judge, synthesis step, and hall-of-fame archive
Missing comparisons to key baselines: no comparison to single-agent LLM approaches (claimed to underperform), related work (RoboMoRe, Text2Robot), or evolutionary alternatives

Reproducibility concerns: references non-existent GPT-5 model, prompts not provided, critical hyperparameters unspecified (debate rounds K, policy training budget, design bounds), no code mentioned, single run reported without multi-seed statistics
Computational cost completely undocumented despite acknowledged scaling with candidates and rounds; no GPU hours or efficiency comparison to alternatives
LLM sensitivity not explored despite acknowledged dependence on prompts and hyperparameters; robustness to different prompt versions and LLM models unknown
Limited design space exploration: only parametric modifications of fixed Ant morphology, cannot add topologies; constrains conclusions about method generality
Insufficient result analysis: morphological changes in Figure 1C unexplained, reward term emergence in Table I not interpreted, claim of diversity lacks quantitative evidence

strengths: Novel multi-agent debate framework combining thesis-antithesis-synthesis structure with simulator-grounded selection for joint morphology-reward co-design—genuinely first work combining these elements

Strong empirical results: 3.2× gains on Ant, ~9× on Swimmer, outperforms RoboMoRe with 36% fewer candidates (80 vs. 125), with learned rewards transferring to 4/5 default morphologies suggesting principled learning

Methodologically sound: crucial separation of training reward from evaluation metric S prevents specification gaming; physics simulation grounds all decisions; two-stage evaluation protocol properly separates search from assessment

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with well-designed ablations (iterative debate shows 18-35% gains over zero-shot, role separation matters, judges improve multi-objective coverage), appropriate statistical analysis with effect sizes for small n=3
Excellent reproducibility: complete prompts in appendices, full hyperparameter documentation, token budgets, costs (~$2.50/run), example debate transcripts, and claim to release code

Strong supporting analyses: critique-action correlation study (χ² tests, all p<0.001) validates judges influence decisions; reward similarity analysis shows D2C discovers structurally different solutions; LLM backbone sensitivity shows framework beats model scale
Clear writing and presentation with informative figures; honest discussion of limitations including computational cost (40 GPU-hours/seed), sim-to-real gap, and limited design space
weaknesses: Limited scope significantly reduces generalizability: only 5 MuJoCo locomotion tasks tested, no manipulation or other domains, no demonstration on non-locomotion problems where debate structure value is unclear
All experiments in simulation without sim-to-real validation; learned morphologies may exploit simulator artifacts; acknowledged but unaddressed limitation reduces practical impact

Computational cost and scalability concerns: ~40 GPU-hours per environment per seed, 5×16=80 RL trainings per seed, unclear scaling to larger design spaces (currently only 6-24 parametric morphology parameters); no early stopping or surrogates discussed

Small sample sizes (n=3 search seeds) limit statistical power; some comparisons non-significant after FDR correction (e.g., HalfCheetah vs. Eureka p=0.1265); final evaluation uses different seeds (5) than search discovery (3 seeds)

Evaluation metric choice (cumulative distance S vs. standard returns) is justified to prevent gaming but introduces design parameter; moderate correlation with standard returns (Spearman ρ=0.61); decoupling leaves interpretability questions

Mixed results for pluralistic judges: limited benefit in inherently stable environments (HalfCheetah, Swimmer), stability judge adds noise in 2D hypervolume tasks (acknowledged), hypervolume gains sometimes marginal

Incomplete analysis of debate mechanism: no ablation on thesis-antithesis-synthesis structure itself, unclear whether gains from critique quality vs. synthesis vs. archive, no analysis of convergence to local optima or failure modes

Reward transferability not universal: fails for Swimmer (4/5 tasks); in Swimmer morphology contributes ~10× leaving little for reward shaping; unclear if transfer generalizes or reflects morphology co-adaptation artifacts

Design choices not fully validated: debate iteration count (5 rounds) unjustified; Nm=4, Nr=4 candidates per round not ablated; judge persona selection (speed/stability/efficiency/novelty) not experimentally validated
Missing evaluation on broader task classes limits ability to claim general benefits of debate structure for design optimization problems

strengths: Comprehensive experimental work with thorough ablations, statistical tests (Welch t-test with FDR correction), and Hedges' g effect sizes demonstrating strong practical significance within evaluated domains
Sensible system design separating training reward r from evaluation metric S to mitigate specification gaming; high reliability (97% code compilation success, 99% fix rate with self-repair)

Novel combination of multi-agent debate with physics-grounded selection and pluralistic judges; critique-parameter co-occurrence analysis demonstrates the feedback mechanism genuinely influences design decisions
Interesting empirical finding of reward transferability to default morphologies (4/5 tasks), suggesting learned principles are not morphology-specific exploits
Well-written presentation with compelling visualizations and detailed appendices (prompts, hyperparameters, cost analysis); example debate transcript effectively illustrates method dynamics
weaknesses: Critical evaluation metric concern: Using cumulative distance S instead of standard episode returns introduces methodological bias. Correlation with standard returns is ρ=0.61 (Spearman) and r=−0.01 (Pearson for Swimmer), raising questions about whether improvements reflect genuine co-design or metric-specific optimization. This choice appears designed to favor D2C.

Questionable baseline comparisons undermine claims: Eureka uses 5 search runs vs D2C's 3 yet D2C is claimed 'more efficient'; RoboMoRe and BO achieve zero scores within authors' Brax-based stack, suggesting implementation issues rather than fundamental limitations; no comparison with state-of-the-art black-box methods (e.g., CMA-ES)

Small sample size (n=3 seeds) severely limits generalizability despite large effect sizes; narrow task scope (5 locomotion benchmarks only, no manipulation/navigation); fixed-topology design space only tunes geometry, not structure
Simulation-only experiments with no sim-to-real validation; morphologies and rewards may exploit simulator artifacts (acknowledged but not addressed)

Incremental novelty over existing work (Eureka + RoboMoRe + standard multi-agent debate literature); core contribution is systems engineering (combining design/control agents + debate structure + pluralistic judges) rather than conceptual breakthrough

Limited understanding of why debate helps: No analysis of why debate surfaces patterns that single-pass generation misses; reward similarity analysis using AST parsing is coarse; discovered principles (wider stance, smoothness penalties) are intuitive rather than revealing new insights
Missing critical ablation: No evaluation of D2C using standard episode returns instead of metric S; unclear whether improvements depend on the specific metric choice
Negative interaction term in Table 1 for Swimmer (Δ_int = −718) inadequately discussed; if morphology dominates over reward for some tasks, this undermines co-design narrative
Ethics statement dismissively avoids discussion of potential harms (adversarial robot design, surveillance, autonomous weapons)
Limited scope for top-tier venue: Only parametric design space, 5 related tasks, simulation-only; no evidence of generalization or transfer beyond MuJoCo benchmarks

strengths: Sound experimental methodology with comprehensive baselines, two-stage evaluation protocol, and careful control of confounds (identical RL budgets and evaluation metrics)
Principled design: separation of training reward r from evaluation score S to avoid specification gaming is well-motivated
Robust implementation quality: 97% reward compilation success, <1% candidate discard, extensive validation checks
Thorough ablation studies isolating contributions from iterative debate, role separation, and pluralistic judges; critique-action correlation analysis provides evidence of judge influence (p<0.001)
Meaningful empirical results: consistent 3.2–9× improvements across 5 tasks; reward transferability to 4/5 default morphologies suggests capture of generalizable principles
Reward transferability claim is substantiated: D2C rewards improve default morphologies in 4/5 tasks without retraining, supporting generalization beyond morphology-specific hacks
Excellent reproducibility support: comprehensive appendices with full prompts, hyperparameters, token budgets, example debate transcripts, and detailed implementation details
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1 overview, debate transcript in G.3)
Honest discussion of limitations and computational costs ($2.50/run, 40 GPU-hours)
Evaluation metric is well-validated: reward-agnostic cumulative distance approach with Spearman ρ=0.61 correlation to standard returns (Appendix H)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: debate mechanism is essentially feedback-driven iterative refinement; underlying techniques (LLM prompting, quality-diversity archives) are well-established; the multi-agent framing packages existing methods rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas

Narrow experimental scope: only 5 locomotion tasks in single domain; parametric morphology changes only (fixed kinematic topology); no manipulation, different gait families, or cross-domain evaluation
Weak statistical power: n=3 search seeds is small; some key comparisons show large p-values (e.g., HalfCheetah vs. Eureka: p=0.127); small-n comparisons inherently uncertain

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: why does debate help beyond 'surfacing novel hypotheses'? What specific failure modes does critique catch? No error analysis comparing design quality/diversity of D2C vs. baselines

Questionable reward transferability claim: on Swimmer (9× morphology gain), rewards show no benefit, contradicting generalization narrative; improvements on HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2D are modest (1.3–1.5×), suggesting morphology-coupling
Sim-to-real gap entirely unaddressed: all experiments in Brax simulation with no robustness validation, domain randomization testing, or hardware deployment
Judges provide feedback only; selection is purely task score S, not arbitrated by LLM judges—framing as 'debate' with judges is somewhat misleading since judges don't arbitrate outcomes
High computational expense ($2.50/run, 40 GPU-hours) limits accessibility and adoption

LLM backbone dependency: proprietary GPT-5.2 with version lock; Appendix I shows 49% failure rate for GPT-5-mini vs. 16% for GPT-5.2, suggesting strong model-quality dependence; archive mechanism masks this inefficiency

Baseline comparisons have fairness concerns: Bayesian Optimization achieves S=0 on some tasks (fundamentally unsuited to discrete design space); RoboMoRe evaluated in D2C's Brax stack; Eureka uses 5 seeds vs. D2C's 3
Design space constraints: fixed topologies limit expressiveness; no topology changes (e.g., adding/removing limbs); parametric bounds are task-specific and manually tuned
Ethical considerations superficial: generic impact statement; no discussion of autonomous weapons, data privacy (LLM API calls), environmental cost, or bias in LLM designs
Missing analyses: ablation on debate round count; sensitivity to hall-of-fame size k; sensitivity to reward function constants; design diversity comparison vs. baselines
Reward similarity metric coarse: AST-based cosine similarity (Appendix D) may not capture functional equivalence
Presentation concerns: judges' role framing is misleading; Figure 2 uses broken y-axis scale complicating comparison
